To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
compensatory, healthcare and family systems can act as obstacles for those with low-back pain to return to work.

the current biopsychological approach to work disability is not enough, as the social and environmental factors that influence work disability due to Low Back Pain have been largely overlooked in the evidence base, and that a whole systems approach is needed to reduce work disability due to chronic pain.
Compensatory, healthcare and family systems can act as obstacles for people with LBP to return to work and remain at work.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a 'whole-system' approach to work disability due to chronic low back pain.
the influence of compensatory, healthcare and family systems on work disability due LBP and how this evidence can be used to inform policy and practice.
the influence of relevant social systems (e.g. family, healthcare, compensatory systems) on work disability due low back pain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is a lack of evidence for the impact of compensatory systems on work disability due LBP, but that there is evidence for how healthcare and family systems act as obstacles to the work participation of those with LBP.
compensatory and healthcare systems have been identified as obstacles, and the role of family systems is less certain.

the evidence suggests that the following features of the systems can act as obstacles: (i) the way in which the compensatory systems are designed and administered; (ii) the way in the healthcare system is designed and administered and; (iii) the way in family systems are designed and managed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current biopsychocial model is not sufficient to tackle work disability due to back pain.
the current policy and practice aimed to tackle work disability due to back pain should be revised to incorporate the role of systems.

there is an evidence base to support that there are a number of systems that may act as obstacles to returning to work following a period of sickness absence due to LBP and that there is a need for a whole-systems approach.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are many ways in which the systems can be obstacles to work participation and that these obstacles can act at the level of the individual, their workplace or their broader community.
there are many factors that influence the return to work of people who have been off work for a period of time due to low back problems.
the biopsychsocial model of low back pain is not enough and needs to be complemented by an understanding of the influence of the systems in which the individual is embedded.
